slides.title: Why should I use GraphQL?
slides.body:
It depends on your use case, but in general, GraphQL has a few key features that stand out. For example, GraphQL enables you to:

- Aggregate data from [multiple UI components](https://graphql.org/learn/queries/#fragments).
- Create a representation of your data that feels familiar and natural ([a graph](https://graphql.org/learn/thinking-in-graphs/#it-s-graphs-all-the-way-down)).
- Ensure that all of your data is [statically typed](https://graphql.org/learn/schema/) and these types inform [what queries the schema supports](https://graphql.org/learn/introspection/).
- [Reduce the need for breaking changes](https://graphql.org/learn/best-practices/#versioning), but utilize a [built-in mechanism for deprecations](https://spec.graphql.org/draft/#sec--deprecated) when you need to.
- Access to a [powerful tooling ecosystem](https://graphql.org/code/#generic-tools) with GUIs, editor integrations, code generation, linting, analytics, and more.

[Our homepage](https://graphql.org/) outlines even more reasons to use GraphQL.

You can try out GraphQL without rewriting your entire application. For instance, starting with a single HTTP request that wraps an existing REST call. Your [GraphQL schema](https://graphql.org/learn/thinking-in-graphs/#shared-language) and [business domain model](https://graphql.org/learn/thinking-in-graphs/#business-logic-layer) can expand gradually. We recommend focusing on one use case at first and only building the part of the schema needed for that.

slides.title: Does GraphQL replace REST?
slides.body:
No, not necessarily. They both handle APIs and can [serve similar purposes](https://graphql.org/learn/thinking-in-graphs/#business-logic-layer) from a business perspective. GraphQL is often considered an alternative to REST, but it’s not a definitive replacement.

GraphQL and REST can actually co-exist in your stack. For example, you can abstract REST APIs behind a [GraphQL server](https://www.howtographql.com/advanced/1-server/). This can be done by masking your REST endpoint into a GraphQL endpoint using [root resolvers](https://graphql.org/learn/execution/#root-fields-resolvers).

For an opinionated perspective on how GraphQL compares to REST, check out [How To GraphQL](https://www.howtographql.com/basics/1-graphql-is-the-better-rest/).

slides.title: Is GraphQL a database language like SQL?
slides.body:
No, but this is a common misconception.

GraphQL is a specification typically used for remote client-server communications. Unlike SQL, GraphQL is agnostic to the data source(s) used to retrieve data and persist changes. Accessing and manipulating data is performed with arbitrary functions called [resolvers](https://graphql.org/learn/execution/). GraphQL coordinates and aggregates the data from these resolver functions, then returns the result to the client. Generally, these resolver functions should delegate to a [business logic layer](https://graphql.org/learn/thinking-in-graphs/#business-logic-layer) responsible for communicating with the various underlying data sources. These data sources could be remote APIs, databases, [local cache](https://graphql.org/learn/caching/), and nearly anything else your programming language can access.

For more information on how to get GraphQL to interact with your database, check out our [documentation on resolvers](https://graphql.org/learn/execution/#root-fields-resolvers).

slides.title: How can I learn GraphQL?
slides.body:
There are many resources available to help you learn GraphQL, including this website. In [our documentation](https://graphql.org/learn/), you’ll find a series of articles that explain essential GraphQL concepts and how they work. Our [Community page](https://graphql.org/community) is full of resources to reference and groups to join.

For more practical guides, visit the [How to GraphQL](https://www.howtographql.com/) fullstack tutorial website. We also have a free online course with edX, [Exploring GraphQL: A Query Language for APIs](https://www.edx.org/course/exploring-graphql-a-query-language-for-apis).

Before you start your learning journey, make sure you know [what an API is](https://www.codenewbie.org/blogs/an-intro-to-apis) and how communication generally works between client and server.

slides.title: Is GraphQL only for React or JavaScript developers?
slides.body:
No, not at all. [GraphQL is a specification](https://spec.graphql.org/) that can be [implemented in any language](https://graphql.org/learn/schema/#type-language). Our [Code page](https://graphql.org/code/) contains a long list of libraries in many different programming languages to help with that.

It’s understandable why you’d think this, though. GraphQL was introduced at a [React conference](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9sc8Pyc51uU) and [GraphQL.js](https://graphql.org/graphql-js/) is one of the most widely used implementations to date. We know this can be confusing, so we’re working to improve our documentation and add more code samples that aren’t written in JavaScript.

slides.title: Reference guide
slides.body: Use this chapter when a question comes up. Official source: [General](https://graphql.org/faq/general/)

slides.title: Is GraphQL frontend or backend?
slides.body: Both. GraphQL specifies how you can [exchange information between client and server](https://www.howtographql.com/basics/3-big-picture/). This includes how the server can indicate [what data and operations are available](https://graphql.org/learn/introspection/), how the client should [format requests](https://graphql.org/learn/queries/), how the server should [execute these queries](https://graphql.org/learn/execution/), and what the client will [receive in response](https://graphql.org/learn/serving-over-http/#response).

slides.title: Does GraphQL use HTTP?
slides.body:
Yes, [GraphQL is typically served over HTTP](https://graphql.org/learn/best-practices/#http). This is largely due to how pervasive the HTTP protocol is in our industry. But it helps that you can try out GraphQL by creating [a single HTTP request](https://graphql.org/faq/general/#why-should-i-use-graphql). Guidelines for setting up a GraphQL server to operate over HTTP are available in our [Serving over HTTP](https://graphql.org/learn/serving-over-http/) documentation.

While HTTP is the most common choice for client-server protocol, it’s not the only one. GraphQL is agnostic to the transport layer. So, for example, you could use [WebSockets](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSockets_API) for GraphQL subscriptions instead of HTTP to consume realtime data.

slides.title: How does GraphQL affect my product’s performance?
slides.body:
On a typical GraphQL backend, every field on every type has a focused, single-purpose function for resolving that value. Also, instead of trying to handle data batching on the client, [GraphQL moves that logic to the server](https://graphql.org/learn/best-practices/#server-side-batching-caching). As a result, there are some inherent performance benefits. Minimizing over-fetching and making [fewer roundtrips to the server](https://graphql.org/learn/queries/#fields) are two of them.

Other performance factors should be considered when building out your GraphQL implementation. For example, it’s possible for a GraphQL service to be ‘chatty’ and repeatedly load data from your database. This is commonly solved by [implementing a batching technique](https://graphql.org/learn/best-practices/#server-side-batching-caching) or [utilizing a tool like DataLoader](https://github.com/graphql/dataloader).

slides.title: What is a GraphQL client and why would I use one?
slides.body:
GraphQL clients can help you handle [queries, mutations,](https://graphql.org/learn/queries/) and [subscriptions](https://spec.graphql.org/draft/#sec-Subscription) to a [GraphQL server](https://www.howtographql.com/advanced/1-server/). They use the underlying structure of a GraphQL API to automate certain processes. This includes batching, UI updates, build-time schema validation, and more.

A list of GraphQL clients in various languages is available on our [Code page](https://graphql.org/code/). There’s also an [in-depth explanation of their benefits](https://www.howtographql.com/advanced/0-clients/) on How To GraphQL.

You don't need a specific client to work with GraphQL, though. You might want to start out by [issuing GraphQL results with a regular HTTP client](https://graphql.org/learn/serving-over-http/). Then later switch to a GraphQL-optimized client as your application grows in complexity.

slides.title: Does GraphQL replace ORMs?
slides.body: No, GraphQL is a specification typically used for remote client-server communications. It's [agnostic to the data source(s) used](https://graphql.org/faq/general/#is-graphql-a-database-language-like-sql) and doesn't implement an object-relational mapping technique. But there are ORMs built specifically for GraphQL. A few of those are listed under the [Services section of our Code page](https://graphql.org/code/?tags=services).

slides.title: Is GraphQL owned by Facebook?
slides.body:
No, GraphQL is governed by the [GraphQL Foundation](https://graphql.org/faq/general/#what-is-the-graphql-foundation).

That said, the specification was originally developed at Facebook and [Facebook is a member](https://foundation.graphql.org/members/) of the GraphQL Foundation. You might notice that some of our [GitHub repositories](https://github.com/graphql/) still have the license listed under Facebook Inc. We're updating those and have already converted major projects, like [GraphiQL](https://github.com/graphql/graphiql/blob/main/LICENSE) and [DataLoader](https://github.com/graphql/dataloader/blob/master/LICENSE), to the new copyright: "Copyright (c) {new Date().getFullYear()} GraphQL Contributors."

slides.title: Who is behind GraphQL?
slides.body:
Many people! The [GraphQL specification and all related projects](http://github.com/graphql/) are open source, so anyone is welcome to [contribute](https://graphql.org/faq/general/#how-can-i-contribute-to-the-specification). That said, there is a structure in place behind the repositories. This exists to resolve conflicts within the community and guiding technical decisions.

The [GraphQL Foundation](https://graphql.org/faq/general/#what-is-the-graphql-foundation) provides most of the oversight for GraphQL. It's made up of [representatives from dozens of different companies](https://foundation.graphql.org/members/).

There are also monthly virtual [GraphQL Working Group (WG)](https://github.com/graphql/graphql-wg) meetings managed by the GraphQL Foundation. These meetings are designed to bring together maintainers of commonly used GraphQL libraries and tools, as well as significant contributors to the GraphQL community. The WG meetings are completely open. Anyone is able to join and [propose items to the agenda](https://github.com/graphql/graphql-wg/blob/main/agendas/).

In the [November 2020 WG meeting](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UybZp9O24Ow), it was announced that GraphQL will have a Technical Steering Committee (TSC) going forward. More on that coming soon.

If this is confusing, don’t worry - there’s a lot going on. To get a more visual, high-level overview, check out the [GraphQL Landscape](https://landscape.graphql.org/).

slides.title: What is the GraphQL Foundation?
slides.body:
The [GraphQL Foundation](https://foundation.graphql.org/faq/) is a neutral foundation that provides governance for GraphQL. This includes vendor-neutral oversight of open-source repositories, funding, events, and more. It's hosted under the [Linux Foundation](https://www.linuxfoundation.org/) and consists of [representatives from dozens of different companies](https://foundation.graphql.org/members/). The idea is that it’s an impartial and open home for the GraphQL community.

You can find out more by visiting [foundation.graphql.org](https://foundation.graphql.org/).

slides.title: Reference guide
slides.body: Use this chapter when a question comes up. Official source: [Best Practices](https://graphql.org/faq/best-practices/)

slides.title: Is GraphQL scalable?
slides.body:
Yes, GraphQL is designed to be scalable and is used by many companies in production under a very high load.

GraphQL comes with some [built-in performance boosts](https://graphql.org/faq/best-practices/#how-does-graphql-affect-my-product-s-performance) that can help. But once you push it to production, you're responsible for scaling it across instances and monitoring performance.

slides.title: Does GraphQL support offline usage?
slides.body:
No, or at least not natively. But there are [GraphQL clients](https://graphql.org/faq/best-practices/#what-is-a-graphql-client-and-why-would-i-need-one) that enable you to build offline-first. They use features designed to perform data operations while offline, such as caching and service workers.

You can find a list of GraphQL clients in various languages on our [Code page](https://graphql.org/code/).

slides.title: What are the security concerns with GraphQL?
slides.body:
Most of the security concerns associated with GraphQL are typical for any API or service. A few examples: SQL injections, Denial of Service (DoS) attacks, or someone abusing flawed authentication. But there are also some attacks specific to GraphQL. For instance, [batching attacks](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/GraphQL_Cheat_Sheet.html#batching-attacks). These attacks can happen as a result of GraphQL allowing you to batch multiple queries (or requests for multiple object instances) in a single network call.

No matter the concern, it’s important to be proactive. There are many ways to securing your GraphQL server. Using a timeout, setting a maximum depth for queries, and throttling queries based on the server time it needs to complete are all potential approaches.

For an overview of common security concerns and how to address them, check out the [Security tutorial on How to GraphQL](https://www.howtographql.com/advanced/4-security/) and [OWASP’s GraphQL Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/GraphQL_Cheat_Sheet.html).

slides.title: How can I set up authorization with GraphQL?
slides.body:
We recommend enforcing authorization behavior in the [business logic layer](https://graphql.org/learn/thinking-in-graphs/#business-logic-layer). That way, you have a single source of truth for authorization.

For a more detailed explanation, go to our [Authorization documentation](https://graphql.org/learn/authorization/).

slides.title: How does authentication work with GraphQL?
slides.body:
You can implement authentication with common patterns, such as [OAuth](https://oauth.net/) or [JWT](https://jwt.io/). There’s nothing special about authentication within the GraphQL specification.

Some [GraphQL libraries](https://graphql.org/code/#language-support) include a specific protocol for authentication as well. Although if you’re working with a pipeline model, we recommend that [GraphQL be placed after all authentication middleware](https://graphql.org/learn/serving-over-http/#web-request-pipeline).

If you’re using [GraphQL.js](https://graphql.org/graphql-js/) to build your API server, we have documentation on [handling authentication with Express middleware](https://graphql.org/graphql-js/authentication-and-express-middleware/).

slides.title: Is GraphQL the right fit for designing a microservice architecture?
slides.body:
Yes, it can be. If you’re integrating GraphQL into your microservice architecture, we’d recommend having one GraphQL schema as an API gateway rather than having your client talk to multiple GraphQL services. This way, you can split your backend into microservices, but then still aggregate all your data to the frontend from a single API.

There are many ways to create an API gateway. The benefit of using GraphQL is that you can take advantage of features like [caching](https://graphql.org/learn/caching/), request budgeting, and planning out query schedules.

slides.title: How does versioning work in GraphQL?
slides.body:
There’s nothing that will prevent a GraphQL service from being versioned like any other REST API. That said, GraphQL avoids versioning by design.

Instead, GraphQL provides the tools to continually build and evolve your schema. For example, GraphQL only returns the data that’s explicitly requested. This means that you can add new features (and all the associated types and fields) without creating a breaking change or bloating results for existing queries.

You can read more about [how versioning works in GraphQL](https://graphql.org/learn/best-practices/#versioning) in our Best Practices section.

slides.title: How can I document my GraphQL API?
slides.body:
One of the benefits of GraphQL is that it's inherently self-documenting. This means that when you use an interactive tool like [GraphiQL](https://github.com/graphql/graphiql), you’re able to explore what data is exposed by your GraphQL API. This includes the [fields](https://graphql.org/learn/queries/#fields), [types](https://graphql.org/learn/schema/#type-system), and more. You can also add a [description field](https://spec.graphql.org/draft/#sec-Documentation) to provide supplementary notes about your endpoint. This description field supports strings and Markdown.

For many, this provides enough API reference documentation. But it doesn’t reduce the need for other forms of documentation. You'll likely still need to create guides that explain how the general concepts tie into your specific use case.

slides.title: Reference guide
slides.body: Use this chapter when a question comes up. Official source: [Specification](https://graphql.org/faq/specification/)

slides.title: What is the best way to follow specification releases?
slides.body:
The latest working draft release of the GraphQL specification can be found at [spec.graphql.org/draft](https://spec.graphql.org/draft/). Previous editions are also available at permalinks that match their [release tag](https://github.com/graphql/graphql-spec/releases).

The entire process behind each release is open source. You can monitor specification proposals by following [pull requests in the graphql-spec repository](https://github.com/graphql/graphql-spec/pulls). You can also watch past GraphQL Working Group discussions about various proposals on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCERcwLeheOXp_u61jEXxHMA).

slides.title: How can I contribute to the GraphQL specification?
slides.body:
GraphQL is still evolving and contributions are very welcome! The specification (including the [latest working draft](https://spec.graphql.org/)) is open source. [Contributor guidelines](https://github.com/graphql/graphql-spec/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) are available on GitHub.

There are more ways to get involved with GraphQL beyond the specification though. Updating the content on [this website and the documentation](https://github.com/graphql/graphql.github.io), for example. Or contributing to [graphql-js](https://github.com/graphql/graphql-js), [graphql-http](https://github.com/graphql/graphql-http), [GraphiQL](https://github.com/graphql/graphiql), or [one of the many other projects](https://github.com/graphql/) maintained by the [GraphQL Foundation](https://graphql.org/faq/specification/#what-is-the-graphql-foundation).

slides.title: What is GraphQL Specification membership?
slides.body:
The [GraphQL Specification](https://specification.graphql.org) and the associated reference implementations are a Joint Development Foundation project (also part of the Linux Foundation family). Individual or corporate contributors sign a document at no cost that they agree their contributions are under the open source licenses of the project. Because this is not GraphQL Foundation membership, specification members do not decide how to spend the budget.

To sign the [GraphQL Specification membership document](https://github.com/graphql/graphql-wg/tree/HEAD/membership), open a PR against any [GraphQL repo on GitHub](https://github.com/graphql).

If your organization uses and benefits from GraphQL, please consider becoming a member of both by opening a PR on behalf of your company and [joining the GraphQL Foundation](https://join.graphql.org).

slides.title: Where is the documentation for subscriptions?
slides.body:
It's not on this website yet, but we're working on it. If you'd like to help write guides on subscriptions, please [let us know](https://github.com/graphql/graphql.github.io/issues/993).

For now, the specification includes details for [how to write and execute subscriptions](https://spec.graphql.org/draft/#sec-Subscription).

slides.title: Reference guide
slides.body: Use this chapter when a question comes up. Official source: [Frontend](https://graphql.org/faq/frontend/)

slides.title: Does GraphQL replace Redux or other state management libraries?
slides.body:
No, GraphQL isn’t a state management library - but it can reduce the need for one.

One benefit of state management libraries like Redux is that they can manipulate API responses into a format that your application understands. With GraphQL, you have control over [what data you request](https://graphql.org/learn/queries/#fields) and typically results are formatted in a client-friendly way by the graph design. So this benefit is already built-in. Many [client libraries](https://graphql.org/faq/frontend/#what-is-a-graphql-client-and-why-would-i-need-one) can also be used to manage state and have features like caching built-in. You may still decide to implement a state management library, but using it to format response data is generally not necessary.

slides.title: Reference guide
slides.body: Use this chapter when a question comes up. Official source: [GraphQL Foundation](https://graphql.org/faq/foundation/)

slides.title: What does the GraphQL Foundation do?
slides.body: The primary responsibility of the Foundation is to set policy and allocate the budget to maximize the sustainability of the GraphQL community. Members participate on a governing board that meets monthly and decides how to allocate its funding.

slides.title: Where does the funding go when I become a member?
slides.body:
The GraphQL Foundation is funded exclusively through the support of our members. The governing board sets an annual budget to use the dues to the maximum benefit of the community.
Ways the Foundation distributes the money raised through memberships include:

- Providing grants and sponsorship to core community developers who are working in neutral roles.
- Funding core community IT infrastructure.
- Funding coordination, financial, and legal support programs for the Foundation and the GraphQL project ecosystem.
- Other community and developer support programs.

The GraphQL Foundation budget is realigned as the needs of the community change.

slides.title: How are decisions made?
slides.body: As with other Linux Foundation projects, the governing board makes decisions through votes. Every vote is equal and no members have special voting rights or privileges. The charter currently limits the governing board to 25 members.

slides.title: Who can join the GraphQL Foundation?
slides.body: GraphQL Foundation membership is open to companies who wish to support the GraphQL ecosystem. As the GraphQL Foundation is hosted at the [Linux Foundation](https://linuxfoundation.org), members must also join the Linux Foundation.

slides.title: Do I need to join the Foundation to participate in GraphQL development?
slides.body:
No, Foundation membership is separate from the technical development community. There is no cost to participate in GraphQL development, although you must sign the [free GraphQL Specification membership agreement](https://github.com/graphql/graphql-wg/tree/main/membership) in order to participate. These two things are different from each other.

Members join the Foundation in order to provide essential funding and participate in the decisions on how it is used. Developers join the GraphQL Specification in order to contribute ideas, code, and other content. Many companies do both.

slides.title: How do I participate in technical development?
slides.body:
We would love to have you! The best place to get started is the [GraphQL Working Group](https://github.com/graphql/graphql-wg/tree/HEAD/membership), which meets monthly. Open a PR to add yourself to the agenda, and you are welcome to join.

Otherwise, you can get involved in [any of our other projects](https://github.com/graphql/graphql-wg/blob/main/GraphQL-TSC.md#about-the-graphql-specification-project).

slides.title: Who founded the organization?
slides.body: The GraphQL Foundation was founded by Apollo, AWS, Butterfly Network, Dgraph Labs, Facebook, Gatsby, GraphZen, Hasura, IBM, Intuit, Neo4j, Novvum, Pipefy, Salsify, Solo.io and Thicit.

slides.title: Who is currently a member?
slides.body: You can learn more about our membership on the [GraphQL Foundation membership page](https://graphql.org/foundation/members).

slides.title: How do we join?
slides.body: You can become a member of GraphQL Foundation and the Linux Foundation by completing our [membership application form](https://join.graphql.org).

slides.title: Project brief
slides.body: Design an API for learners browsing courses, enrolling, completing lessons and viewing progress. Create schema.graphql, operations.graphql and a design note. You may implement it locally using [the current GraphQL.js tutorial](https://www.graphql-js.org/docs/). The LMS does not execute your project.

slides.title: Schema and operations
slides.body: Define Course, Lesson, Enrollment and structured mutation inputs. Model a bounded course connection, a course lookup and an enrollment lookup. Write named queries with variables, reusable fragments, an enroll mutation and a completion mutation. State whether progress updates require a subscription or polling.

slides.title: Error and access cases
slides.body: Specify course-not-found, full-course and forbidden-access behavior. Write a valid request, an invalid field selection and a resolver failure with partial data. Trace non-null propagation. Test that changing an enrollment ID cannot reveal another learner’s data.

slides.title: Performance and evolution
slides.body: Explain where N+1 occurs and how request-scoped batching fixes it. Set pagination and demand limits. Propose a migration replacing title with displayTitle. Include a schema diff, consumer checks, owner approval and rollout/rollback notes.

slides.title: Self-review rubric
slides.body: Award 0–2 points for each: valid schema/types; queries/variables/fragments; clear writes/outcomes; identity and access control; pagination/performance; failure handling; evolution/governance; documented tradeoffs. Target 13/16. This is a manual review and does not produce a verified certificate.

slides.title: Normative reference
slides.body: Read [GraphQL September 2025](https://spec.graphql.org/September2025/). The specification defines the language and type system; official best practices offer operational guidance. New proposals and draft behavior must be checked against your implementation.

slides.title: Reference map
slides.body:
Language → documents, operations, fields, arguments, fragments, directives and variables.
Type System → schemas, scalar/object/interface/union/enum/input types, wrappers and directives.
Validation → document correctness before execution.
Execution → coercion, field collection, query/mutation/subscription execution and error propagation.
Response → data, errors and extensions.
Appendices → grammar and supporting reference.

slides.title: Final preparation
slides.body: Revisit the objective and worked check for each chapter. Complete the capstone self-review, then attempt the final assessment. Explain why each correct answer is correct; use its cited chapter if you are unsure.

questions.prompt: What does a GraphQL schema define?
questions.explanation: Schemas describe the API contract, independent of storage.

questions.prompt: Which type can be used for structured mutation arguments?
questions.explanation: Input objects are designed for structured input values.

questions.prompt: What does [Lesson!]! permit?
questions.explanation: Neither list nor item may be null; an empty list is still valid.

questions.prompt: How should dynamic user values be passed?
questions.explanation: Variables separate runtime values from the document.

questions.prompt: What do aliases change?
questions.explanation: Aliases name the response entries, including repeated fields with different arguments.

questions.prompt: Which fields execute serially in a mutation?
questions.explanation: Serial root execution does not imply a database transaction.

questions.prompt: What does a subscription provide?
options: A guarantee of a particular WebSocket protocol
An event stream with a selection executed per event
questions.explanation: Transport and lifecycle details are implementation concerns.

questions.prompt: When does schema validation occur?
questions.explanation: Validation rejects invalid documents before executing resolvers.

questions.prompt: A non-null field fails. What happens?
options: Null propagates to the nearest nullable ancestor
The failed field becomes an empty string
questions.explanation: The error is recorded; the response follows nullability boundaries.

questions.prompt: Which response requires partial-data handling?
options: A response containing both data and errors
questions.explanation: Execution can produce usable data alongside field errors.

questions.prompt: What does __typename return?
options: The field value type as JSON
The concrete runtime object type name
questions.explanation: This meta field helps discriminate union/interface results.

questions.prompt: Where do wrapper type details appear in introspection?
questions.explanation: NON_NULL and LIST wrappers refer to their wrapped type through ofType.

questions.prompt: Which concern is outside the core language specification?
questions.explanation: Operational policy belongs to the application.

questions.prompt: Which schema is easiest for consumers to understand?
options: One mirroring every database join table
One based on meaningful business relationships
One exposing only generic string blobs
questions.explanation: Model the domain and document semantics.

questions.prompt: How can a full-course enrollment rejection be represented?
questions.explanation: Expected business outcomes can be modeled as data.

questions.prompt: What should a client do with an unknown enum value?
options: Treat it as permission to access all data
questions.explanation: Remote schemas evolve; fallbacks protect clients.

questions.prompt: What should happen before removing a deprecated field?
options: Delete it immediately after adding a reason
questions.explanation: Deprecation communicates intent; removal needs evidence and coordination.

questions.prompt: Which request must not execute via GET?
questions.explanation: The HTTP guidance prohibits mutation execution through GET.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended file-upload pattern?
options: Put every large binary inside a JSON variable
Trust the supplied filename as proof of file type
Authorize a signed URL, upload to storage, then associate the object
questions.explanation: Signed URLs reduce upload handling burdens; validation and ownership checks still matter.

questions.prompt: Where should object access rules be enforced?
options: In trusted business logic using caller identity
questions.explanation: Authorization must protect underlying actions and objects.

questions.prompt: What should a client pass as after for the next page?
options: A guessed database offset encoded as a cursor
questions.explanation: Treat cursor values as opaque and use pageInfo.

questions.prompt: What does a global object ID guarantee by itself?
questions.explanation: Authorization remains necessary for node lookups.

questions.prompt: What is the first step when a server cannot parse the request JSON?
options: Check HTTP body format and media types
questions.explanation: Transport parsing happens before GraphQL validation and execution.

questions.prompt: What usually identifies a normalized cache object?
options: Its position in the last list
Stable identity such as __typename plus id
questions.explanation: Stable identity merges representations of the same object.

questions.prompt: How can N+1 author lookups be reduced?
options: Batch IDs with a request-scoped loader
questions.explanation: Batching reduces repeated backend calls; scope caches to authorization boundaries.

questions.prompt: Which is a layered demand-control strategy?
options: Bound pagination, cost and rate with timeouts
questions.explanation: Multiple controls address different sources of work.

questions.prompt: What is federation?
options: A mandatory feature of every GraphQL server
Composition of domain subgraphs behind a unified API
questions.explanation: Composition and query planning are ecosystem capabilities with implementation-specific rules.

questions.prompt: What should schema ownership specify?
options: Only the color of schema diagrams
questions.explanation: Explicit ownership makes decisions and escalation practical.

questions.prompt: What does a schema registry replace?
options: It does not replace human review
questions.explanation: Registries support workflow, history and usage evidence.

questions.prompt: Which proposed field needs review for operational risk?
options: An unbounded nested list without access rules
questions.explanation: Review pagination, authorization, nullability and backend work.

questions.prompt: What is a safer field migration sequence?
options: Add, deprecate, migrate, monitor, then remove by policy
questions.explanation: Plan compatibility and rollback using consumer evidence.
